1380.title: R-Ch-M
1380.hook: rachamim, mercy, shares a root with rechem, womb
1380.howItsDone: Jewish prayer calls God ha-Rachaman, the Merciful One, and in the grace after meals a series of requests each begins with that name; rachamim, mercy, is asked for throughout the daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, N-Ch-M: nachamu, comfort ye, and Joseph speaking to his brothers' hearts. Your line was comfort. Today, a root that starts deeper in the body.

Two women stand before King Solomon with one baby between them. They share a house; each had a son; one child died in the night, and now each says the living one is hers. No witnesses. No proof. The king calls for a sword and gives an order that makes the whole court go still: divide the living child in two, and give half to each. One woman breaks. The King James says it in old, physical words: "for her bowels yearned upon her son." The other says, let it be neither mine nor yours. What moves inside the first woman is today's root.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE BABY.` → `BRING ME A SWORD.` → `HER BOWELS YEARNED UPON HER SON.`

segments.voice: R-Ch-M. Resh, chet, mem. Turn it four ways. First, the body. Voice these letters one way and you have rechem, the womb. Voice them another way and you have rachamim, mercy, compassion. The same letters hold the place a child grows and the feeling that protects it. Second, back to the courtroom. What the King James calls bowels is, in Hebrew, her rachamim, stirring. And look at what that mercy does. She gives up her own claim: give her the living child, she says, and in no wise slay it. She would rather lose him to the other woman than to the sword. Solomon hears it and knows at once who the mother is. Mercy is the evidence. Third, not only mothers. A psalm uses the root for a father: "Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him." Pitieth is racham. The womb-love picture stretches to anyone who loves the way a parent loves, and then again, to God. Fourth, a name for God. Jewish prayer calls God ha-Rachaman, the Merciful One; in the grace after meals, a run of short requests each opens with that word. Sitting at a table, full, people address God by a name built from a womb. So mercy here isn't a cool decision handed down from a bench. It's the feeling that rises from the gut when someone small is in danger, and acts before thinking.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's let you down lately, not badly, just enough to sting, and picture them small, five years old in a kitchen doorway, trying and failing. Let the feeling shift if it wants to, and ask what a loving parent would say to that child: not excuses, just mercy. If you pray, you can ask the Merciful One for mercy for them, and for yourself.
R-Ch-M. Resh, chet, mem: rechem, the womb, and rachamim, mercy, the love that protects what it carries. Today's word.
Your line: mercy is womb-love. It protects what it carries. See you tomorrow.

1381.title: Ch-N-N
1381.hook: chen, grace; chanun, gracious, in the thirteen attributes
1381.howItsDone: Jews chant the thirteen attributes of mercy, drawn from Exodus 34:6–7, aloud on fast days and during the High Holy Days, and the priestly blessing asks that God 'be gracious unto thee'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, R-Ch-M: rechem and rachamim, the womb and mercy, and a mother at Solomon's court. Your line was mercy is womb-love. Today, the word that stands right next to mercy on the mountain.

The first tablets lie broken at the foot of the mountain, smashed after the golden calf. Moses makes a bold request: "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." The answer is no, and yes. No face. But God will pass by while Moses stands hidden in a cleft of the rock, and God will call out names. So Moses climbs again, carrying two new stone tablets. When it happens, he doesn't see a shape. He hears a list. And right beside mercy in that list stands today's root.
screen: `SHEW ME THY GLORY.` → `TWO NEW TABLETS.` → `NOT A FACE: A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Ch-N-N. Chet, nun, nun. Chen, grace, favor. Chanun, gracious. Turn it four ways. First, an earlier verse. As the flood story opens, the world has gone bad, and then comes a short line: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Grace there is chen. Notice the order: the verse gives no reason first; only after it does the text call Noah a just man. Some readers hear that as the shape of grace: favor that arrives before anyone earns it. Second, back on the mountain. God passes by and proclaims: "The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth." Merciful is rachum, from yesterday's root. Gracious is chanun, from today's. The two stand side by side, as if one needs the other. Third, the priestly blessing from a few days ago, one line further on: "The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee." The same root, asked for every time it's said. Fourth, the list said aloud, which you met in year two. Tradition counts the qualities Moses heard as thirteen attributes, and congregations chant them together on fast days and in the season of the High Holy Days. A people asking to be forgiven reaches for the words God used just after the golden calf. So grace in this root isn't a reward. It's the extra that's given when nothing is owed.

segments.voice: Look ahead at the rest of your day for a moment when someone is owed exactly nothing from you: the driver trying to merge, the slow cashier, the one who apologized badly. Decide now to give a little more than the rule requires, room, patience, a real thank-you, a pass, and see it happen. If you pray, you can ask, in the words of the blessing, that God be gracious to you, and to them.
Ch-N-N. Chet, nun, nun: chen, grace, the favor Noah found, and chanun, gracious, standing beside merciful in the attributes. Today's word.
Your line: grace. On the mountain, it stands right beside mercy. See you again tomorrow.

1382.title: Y-D-A
1382.carry: to know is to be close
1382.howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers note that the Hebrew verb yada, to know, is used in the Bible for intimacy and relationship as well as for facts, and da'at, knowledge, is a word that recurs in Jewish prayer and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-N-N: chen, grace, the favor Noah found, given when nothing is owed. Today, a root about knowing.

A doctor can know your chart cover to cover and still not know you. A neighbor of many years can know your name, your car and your trash day, and nothing else. English uses one verb for all of it. Hebrew has a verb for knowing too, and in the Bible it keeps turning up where English would reach for a warmer word. A garden. A marriage. A name spoken by God. Three letters, yud, dalet, ayin: Y-D-A. And a simple question: what does it take to really know someone?
screen: `THE CHART, NOT THE PERSON.` → `ONE VERB IN ENGLISH.` → `Y-D-A: TO KNOW.`

segments.voice: Y-D-A gives yada, to know, and da'at, knowledge. Turn it four ways. First, the garden. In the middle of Eden stands "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." Knowledge there is da'at, and in the story it isn't something you look up. You take it in, eat it, carry it inside you. Second, the marriage. Two chapters later: "And the man knew Eve his wife." Yada, for the closest two people can be. In the Bible's Hebrew, knowing can mean intimacy. Third, the name. Moses asks to be shown God's ways, and the answer comes: "thou hast found grace in My sight, and I know thee by name." Grace, yesterday's word, sits right beside knowing. To be known by name is to be held close, not filed away. Fourth, the hope. Jeremiah describes a day when no one will need to teach a neighbor about God, "for they shall all know Me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them." Not know about. Know. Some Jewish teachers read that as a relationship more than a fact, the way you know a friend's laugh across a crowded room. So the root always asks: arm's length, or up close? The neighbor who knows your trash day has information. The friend who can tell why you're quiet today has da'at.

segments.voice: Bring one person to mind, someone you see often but know only at arm's length: a coworker, a cousin, the person behind the counter. Notice what you know, a name, a habit, and then what you don't: what makes them laugh, who they miss, how their week has really gone. Let one real question for them take shape, and if you pray, bring their name with you into the quiet.
Y-D-A. Yud, dalet, ayin: the root of yada, to know, and da'at, knowledge, where knowing can mean closeness. Today's word.
Your line: to know is to be close. In the Bible's Hebrew, knowing was never only facts. See you tomorrow.

1383.title: Children and builders (Berakhot 64a)
1383.hook: the rabbis read banayich, your children, as bonayich, your builders
1383.howItsDone: The passage from the end of tractate Berakhot, with its reading of banayich as bonayich, is printed in some prayer books and is quoted at some celebrations of learning, such as the completion of a tractate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-D-A: yada, knowing up close, the verb for a fact, a friend and a marriage. Today, one word read two ways.

On a living-room rug, a kid is stacking blocks. Red on blue, a yellow one balanced on top, a tower that leans and somehow holds. An adult walks past and sees a mess to tidy before dinner. The kid sees a city. Who's right? The Talmud has an answer, and it hides in a single vowel. Near the close of Berakhot, the tractate of blessings, a rabbi quotes Isaiah's verse about children and reads one word of it a second way. Same letters, different sound.
screen: `A KID, A TOWER OF BLOCKS.` → `A MESS, OR A CITY?` → `ONE WORD, READ TWICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And all thy children shall be taught of the LORD; And great shall be the peace of thy children." Turn it four ways. First, the word. Thy children, in Hebrew, is banayich: ben, a son, a child, with the ending that means yours. Second, the move. In Berakhot, Rabbi Elazar, in the name of Rabbi Chanina, says that students of the wise increase peace in the world, and quotes this verse. Then he adds: don't read banayich, your children. Read bonayich, your builders. Without vowel marks, the way it stands in a scroll, the two look alike. Only the sound changes. Third, the kind of move. The rabbis call it al tikri, don't read. It doesn't erase the plain meaning; Isaiah still says children. The second reading stands beside the first, like a harmony over a melody: your children will be taught, and your builders will have great peace. Fourth, who the builders are. In the passage, they're the ones who learn. A child taught today is already laying stones for a peace not yet built. Back to the rug. The adult sees a mess. The Talmud, reading Isaiah, sees a builder learning how a thing holds, and that learning, says Berakhot, is how peace gets built.
screen: `BANAYICH: YOUR CHILDREN.` · `READ IT BONAYICH: YOUR BUILDERS.` · `AL TIKRI: A SECOND READING BESIDE.` · `THE LEARNERS BUILD THE PEACE.` · then, large: `בניך`

segments.voice: Bring one child to mind: your own, a niece, a student, a kid down the street, or, if no child comes, the child you once were. Picture them building something, a tower, a drawing, a question they keep asking, and see the thing they made rather than the mess around it. Find one sentence of encouragement about the building, not about being good, and if you pray, hold their name in the quiet.
Children and builders. Banayich and bonayich: one set of letters in Isaiah, read two ways in the Talmud, so that the children are the builders. Today's word.
Your line: children are builders. Same letters, two readings, both standing at once. Same time tomorrow.

1384.title: K-B-D
1384.howItsDone: Kibbud av va'em, honoring father and mother, is a commandment Jews study and practice in detail; and the word kavod, honor, is used in daily Jewish life for the respect owed to every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, children and builders: banayich read as bonayich, the kid on the rug laying stones for peace. Today, a root you can feel in your arms.

Some people leave a meeting and nobody notices the empty chair. Others step out for a minute and the whole room goes off balance, as if something heavy has been lifted off the table. English says it too: his word carries weight. We talk about importance as if it had mass. Hebrew builds the idea into a root. The same three letters that mean heavy also mean honor. Kaf, vet, dalet: K-B-D.
screen: `THE ROOM GOES OFF BALANCE.` → `HIS WORD CARRIES WEIGHT.` → `K-B-D: HEAVY, AND HONOR.`

segments.voice: Turn it four ways. First, heavy. Israel is fighting Amalek, and Moses stands on a hill with his hands raised. While they're up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek does. "But Moses' hands were heavy." Heavy is kaved, from this root. So Aaron and Hur put a stone under him to sit on and hold up his hands, one on each side, until the sun goes down. Second, honor. "Honour thy father and thy mother." Honor is kabed, the very same letters. To honor a parent, in the root's own picture, is to treat them as heavy: not easy to brush aside. Third, glory. When Moses goes up Sinai, "the glory of the LORD abode upon mount Sinai," and a cloud covers the mountain. Glory is kavod: presence that settles and doesn't drift off. Fourth, the twist. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma, whom you met on day two hundred sixty-five asking who is wise, asks: who is honored? The one who honors other people. You don't get weight by demanding it. You get it by giving it. A tired man's arms, a parent, a cloud, a sage's question. Honor, in Hebrew, isn't a title. It's how much someone weighs to you: whether their words land, or blow away.
screen: `HEAVY: MOSES' HANDS.` · `HONOR: THY FATHER AND THY MOTHER.` · `GLORY: THE CLOUD ON SINAI.` · `WHO IS HONORED? WHO HONORS OTHERS.` · then, large: `כָּבוֹד`

Bring to mind someone whose words you tend to skim, a parent, a coworker, an older neighbor who tells the same story twice, and recall one thing they said lately. This time let it land and weigh what it weighs, and if you pray, hold them in the quiet.
K-B-D. Kaf, vet, dalet: the root of kaved, heavy, and kavod, honor and glory. To honor is to give weight. Today's word.

1385.title: Tz-L-M
1385.hook: tzelem, image, as in the image of God
1385.howItsDone: Jewish teaching draws on tzelem Elohim, the image of God in every person, when it speaks about human dignity; the Mishnah's teaching about one seal and no two faces alike is studied as part of tractate Sanhedrin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, K-B-D: honor as weight, and Moses' tired hands held up on the hill. Today, a root about faces.

Rush hour. A train car packed shoulder to shoulder. A man asleep against the window, mouth open. A teenager with headphones and a scowl. A woman doing her makeup in her phone's camera. Someone humming, someone crying quietly behind sunglasses. Nobody looks at anybody. The first chapter of Genesis makes a claim about every one of those faces, in one short word. Tzadi, lamed, mem: Tz-L-M. Tzelem. Image.
screen: `A PACKED TRAIN CAR.` → `NOBODY LOOKS AT ANYBODY.` → `TZ-L-M: IMAGE.`

segments.voice: You met this verse on day twenty-four; today, the word inside it. First: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them." Tzelem, twice, and then a line so nobody misses who's included: male and female. Second, what the word names elsewhere. In other books, tzelem can mean a statue, like the images of Baal that the people of the land break in pieces in the book of Kings. A tzelem stands for someone. So Genesis takes a word for a carved figure and uses it for a person made of dust and breath. Third, the coins. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, says: a human king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all come out alike. God stamped every person with the seal of the first human, and not one is like another. Fourth, what follows. After the flood, God tells Noah that whoever sheds a person's blood will answer for it, "for in the image of God made He man." Harm a person, and you've struck at the image. Rabbi Akiva, in Pirkei Avot, adds a softer line: a human is beloved, created in the image, and more beloved still that it was made known to him. Back to the train car. Genesis doesn't say those faces are nice, or right, or easy to sit next to. It says each one carries the image.

Notice one thing about it that no other face has, a crease, a habit, the way they stand: one seal, and no two alike. Stay with that face for a few breaths, and if you pray, hold that person in the quiet.
Tz-L-M. Tzadi, lamed, mem: tzelem, image, the word Genesis uses for every human being made in the image of God. Today's word.
Your line: the image. Even the scowler by the window carries it. Rest well.

1386.title: D-B-R
1386.hook: davar is both a word and a thing; midbar, the desert, shares the letters
1386.howItsDone: Jews call the fifth book of the Torah Devarim, words, and the fourth Bemidbar, in the wilderness, from words near their openings; Jewish ethics treats speech seriously, with whole bodies of law about promises, vows and harmful talk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tz-L-M: tzelem, the image, one seal and no two faces alike. Today closes the week, with a root about words themselves.

Look back at this week's words. Rachamim, mercy, from the word for womb. Chen, grace. Yada, knowing up close. Banayich read as bonayich, children as builders. Kavod, honor as weight. Tzelem, the image in every face. Six days, each one a word on a screen and a sound in your ear. Fair question at the end of a week like that: are words just air and ink? Hebrew answers with a root that won't keep the two apart. Dalet, bet, resh: D-B-R.
screen: `MERCY, GRACE, KNOWING.` → `BUILDERS, WEIGHT, THE IMAGE.` → `ARE WORDS JUST WORDS?`

segments.voice: D-B-R gives davar, and davar means two things at once: a word, and a thing. First, one verse with both: "After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram." Things is devarim. Word is davar. The same root twice in one line, and English needs two words to carry it. Second, a book named for it. Deuteronomy, in Hebrew, is Devarim, from its opening: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan; in the wilderness." Third, that wilderness. It's midbar, spelled with a mem in front of the same three letters. The book of Numbers is called Bemidbar, in the wilderness. Some readers hear something in that: the empty place is where the words came. The Torah is given in the desert. Fourth, words that make things. "By the word of the LORD were the heavens made." In Genesis, God says, let there be light, and there is light. In this root, a word is never only air. Once it's said, it's a thing in the world, doing something. A promise is a thing. So is an insult, so is a blessing, and so is a sentence of encouragement for a child. This week's words were each meant to become something.
screen: `AFTER THESE THINGS, THE WORD.` · `DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.` · `MIDBAR: THE WILDERNESS, SAME LETTERS.` · `BY THE WORD WERE THE HEAVENS MADE.` · then, large: `דָּבָר`

segments.voice: Let the week's words pass by once, slowly, mercy, grace, knowing, builders, weight, image, and notice which one stays a little longer than the others. Give that one a body: if it's mercy, who could use some; if it's weight, whose words could land. Picture the deed, small and specific, a call, a note, a door held open, and if you pray, carry the word into the quiet.
D-B-R. Dalet, bet, resh: davar, a word and a thing at once; the letters inside midbar, the wilderness. Today's word.
Your line: words are things. Davar: the word and the thing, one root. A new week starts tomorrow.
